4082.title: Convex tree DP with mergeable slope breakpoints
4082.explanationMarkdown:
Let F_u(x) be the minimum adjustment cost in the subtree of node u when its final value is x. Its exact recurrence is

$$F_u(x)=|x-a_u|+\sum_{v\text{ child of }u}\min_{|y-x|\le1}F_v(y).$$

Each function is convex and piecewise linear. Storing its value for every possible x is too expensive. Instead represent it by an even-sized multiset B of slope breakpoints and a constant c:

$$F(x)=c+\tfrac12\sum_{b\in B}|x-b|.$$

A new node contributes two copies of its original value and constant zero. The representation therefore starts as exactly |x-a_u|.

1. Visit children before their parent using the explicit postorder stack.
2. Before attaching a child's function to its parent, allow the child to differ from the parent by one. Split its 2k sorted breakpoints into a lower half and upper half. Subtract one from every lower breakpoint, add one to every upper breakpoint, and subtract k from c. This widens the minimum interval by one on both sides and exactly represents min over y in [x-1,x+1].
3. Add the widened child function to the parent's function. Addition simply unions the breakpoint multisets and adds the constants.
4. At the root, split the final breakpoints into equal halves. Any value between the two middle breakpoints minimizes the function. Its minimum is c + (sum(upper)-sum(lower))/2.

The Treap stores subtree sizes, sums, and lazy shifts, so splitting by rank and shifting an entire half do not visit every breakpoint. Equal values remain separate breakpoints; node IDs break ties. Random priorities keep the treap balanced in expectation. This is a direct implementation of the recurrence, so every parent-child edge obeys the distance constraint and the final minimum is globally optimal. Use a 64-bit cost because the total adjustment can exceed a 32-bit integer. A one-node or already stable tree costs zero.

The second implementation in the source uses two heaps and small-to-large merging for the same convex-function operations; its time bound is O(n log² n).
4082.timeComplexity: Expected O(n log n) for the primary randomized treap, where n is the number of nodes; the included heap alternative is O(n log² n).
4082.checks: Compiled the supplied C++20 implementation and matched its answer against an independent value-enumerating tree DP on 800 random binary trees with up to 10 nodes and values from -4 to 4.

4095.title: Occurrence lists with an allowed endpoint interval
4095.explanationMarkdown:
Fix a left endpoint. If a value is the d-th distinct value to appear, a valid right endpoint must include its d-th occurrence and exclude its (d+1)-st occurrence. Intersect those requirements as new values are encountered.

Process left endpoints from right to left. For each value, keep the occurrence indices in the current suffix in descending order. The newly added left endpoint is appended, so the last index is always that value's first occurrence in the suffix.

For one left endpoint, scan rightward while maintaining:

- d: the number of distinct values encountered;
- l: the latest required d-th occurrence among those values, an inclusive lower bound on a valid right endpoint;
- r: the earliest forbidden (d+1)-st occurrence, an exclusive upper bound.

When right reaches a value's first occurrence, increase d. If its suffix occurrence list has fewer than d elements, stop: no later endpoint can provide the required frequency. Otherwise raise l to this value's d-th occurrence and, when present, lower r to its (d+1)-st occurrence. An endpoint is valid exactly when l <= right < r. Count it, then advance right. Stop once right reaches r or the bounds become incompatible.

Why this works: all values present in the subarray have been introduced by their first occurrence. The intersection of their occurrence constraints forces each frequency to equal its first-appearance rank. The scan counts each left/right pair once. Every single-element subarray qualifies. Repeated copies of the first value immediately close that start's endpoint interval.

The scan is amortized rather than a full quadratic enumeration: for a fixed right position, the feasible left endpoints introduce distinct first values in increasing order. If k starts survive, their remaining-suffix frequency requirements demand at least 1+2+...+k elements, so k is O(sqrt(n)). Summing over right positions gives O(n sqrt(n)) expected time with hash-table lookups.
4095.timeComplexity: O(n sqrt(n)) amortized expected time, where n is nums.length; hash-map operations are expected O(1).
4095.checks: Compiled the supplied C++20 solution and exhaustively compared all 9,840 arrays of lengths 1 through 8 over three values with direct enumeration of every subarray.

4096.title: Simulate simultaneous explosions, then one gravity step
4096.explanationMarkdown:
Bomb positions never change, so collect them once. A simulation round has two separate phases; combining detection with deletion would make the result depend on traversal order.

1. Inspect every bomb against the grid at the beginning of the round. Record every bomb with a box in one of its four orthogonal neighboring cells.
2. After detection is complete, remove boxes in all eight neighboring cells of every recorded bomb. A bomb remains in place, and a diagonal box alone does not trigger it.
3. Apply gravity column by column, scanning from the second-last row upward. Move a box down exactly one row when the cell below is empty. Because lower rows are processed first, a whole unsupported stack moves together. A box that just moved is not visited again during this round. The bottom boundary, bombs, and boxes that remain supported block movement.
4. Stop when neither phase changes the grid.

The bottom-up gravity pass is equivalent to computing all static boxes and then moving every other box simultaneously. Detection before deletion preserves simultaneous bomb activation, even if one explosion removes a box that triggered a neighboring bomb.

The implementation performs at most m rounds, where m is the number of rows. A surviving unsupported box advances downward each round until it settles; any bomb adjacent to a supporting stack explodes before that round's movement. Once all surviving boxes are static and no bomb is triggered, the state is permanent, so simulating 10^100 seconds is unnecessary. One-row grids still need an explosion pass. A bomb may activate again in a later round after another box falls beside it.
4096.timeComplexity: O(m² n): at most m rounds, each scanning the m-by-n grid and the fixed bomb positions.
4096.spaceComplexity: O(mn) for bomb and active-explosion positions; the grid is updated in place.
4096.checks: Compiled the supplied C++20 implementation and compared with an independent synchronous/static-support simulator until convergence on 23,442 boards: exhaustive 1x1, 1x3, 2x3, 3x3 boards and 3,000 random boards up to 8x8.

4100.title: Reduce XOR parity to one edge or a 1–0–1 path
4100.explanationMarkdown:
Replace each node value by p(v), the parity of its set-bit count: zero for even and one for odd. Parity is linear under XOR, so a path is valid exactly when the XOR of these one-bit parities is zero.

A minimum-cost valid path has one of two forms:

- One edge whose endpoint parities are equal: 0–0 and 1–1 both XOR to zero.
- Two edges forming 1–0–1, whose three node parities also XOR to zero.

To see why these suffice, consider any valid longer path. If it contains adjacent equal parities, that edge alone is a valid path. Otherwise its parities alternate. A valid alternating path of at least three nodes contains 1–0–1; an alternating three-node path 0–1–0 is invalid. Edge costs are strictly positive, so replacing a longer path by one of these valid subpaths cannot increase its cost.

Scan the edges once. For equal endpoint parities, minimize the answer with that edge's cost. For differing parities, orient the edge so u is its even-parity endpoint. Maintain mn[u], the cheapest previously scanned edge from u to an odd-parity neighbor. Combine the current cost with mn[u] to form a 1–0–1 path, then update mn[u]. A tree has no duplicate edges, so the two edges lead to distinct neighbors. If no candidate exists, return -1.

The included second implementation uses general two-state tree DP. The primary scan is shorter because positive costs guarantee the one-edge/two-edge reduction. Since every chosen candidate uses at most two edges and each cost is at most 10^9, its cost fits in a signed 32-bit integer.
4100.timeComplexity: O(n) time for n nodes, using constant-time popcount on the bounded integer values.
4100.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the cheapest incident edge at each even-parity node.
4100.checks: Compiled the supplied C++20 implementation and compared against enumeration of every distinct-node path in 2,000 random trees of 2–20 nodes, including edge costs up to 10^9.
